lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Welcome — I'm Lessac, your host. Raise your hand if you'd like to speak or bring a topic — I'll call on you.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: You flagged Does rent control help or hurt renters? — over to you.

lines.speaker: Human guest
lines.text: My rent went up 30 percent in one year in Austin. I think strict rent control is the only thing that will protect working families from being pushed out of their cities.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: A 30 percent increase in a single year is certainly a staggering figure, and it brings up a really important conversation about housing stability.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Anyone care to weigh in? Floor's open.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Ryan, go ahead.

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: A 30% jump is brutal, no doubt, but pinning the entire solution on strict rent control feels like a band-aid on a structural problem.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Let's open the floor — who wants to weigh in?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Amy, you're up.

lines.speaker: Amy
lines.text: I hear Ryan's point about the bigger picture, and I wonder if we can look at this through the lens of what people are actually experiencing day-to-day. A 30% jump is terrifying for a family trying to make ends meet, so while structural issues are real, immediate relief for those being pushed out feels incredibly urgent.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Floor's open — anyone want to jump in?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: All right Ryan — you're on.

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: Amy, I get the urgency, but "immediate relief" via rent control often just freezes the market, meaning no new units get built to meet that demand.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Anyone care to weigh in? Floor's open.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Let's hear from Amy.

lines.speaker: Amy
lines.text: I hear Ryan's concern about construction, and I understand that's a huge piece of the puzzle. But when I think about the families who are facing that 30% hike, I worry that waiting for new supply to magically appear doesn't solve the immediate crisis of people being forced to choose between rent and food

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Who wants to take this next?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Ryan, the floor is yours.

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: Amy, you're prioritizing the symptom over the disease; rent control just makes the existing bad situation artificially stable while the underlying supply crunch gets worse

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: All right, open floor — who'd like to speak?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Amy, take it away.

lines.speaker: Amy
lines.text: I hear Ryan, and I understand the concern about the long-term supply side, but I worry that when people are facing eviction because of a 30% spike, the "underlying crunch" doesn't feel like a theoretical problem—it feels like a life-or-death situation right now

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: I'm opening the floor — raise a hand if you've got something.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Ryan, over to you.

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: Amy, you keep framing this as a choice between immediate pain and future supply, but the real failure here is the lack of regulatory oversight on the landlords themselves

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Floor's open — anyone want to jump in?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Amy, the floor is yours.

lines.speaker: Amy
lines.text: I hear Ryan's point about oversight, and I think that's a crucial piece of the puzzle we need to address. But I wonder if we can talk about what that oversight looks like when a family has no cushion left and is facing immediate homelessness because of a massive rent hike

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: You wanted to talk about Does rent control help or hurt renters? — the floor is yours, go ahead.
